## Understanding the problem

Design a structure supporting add(point), which records a point while keeping duplicates distinct, and count(point), which returns how many ways three stored points together with the query point form an axis-aligned square of positive area. The query point acts as a corner of the square.

Key geometry: given query q = (qx, qy), a stored point p = (px, py) is the diagonal corner of some square iff px ≠ qx and |px − qx| = |py − qy| = d > 0. The other two corners are then forced: (px, qy) and (qx, py). With multiplicities m(p), m((px,qy)), m((qx,py)), the diagonal p accounts for the product of the three counts.

Example walkthrough: after adding (3,10), (11,2), (3,2), querying (11,10) finds diagonal (3,2) with side 8; corners (11,2) and (3,10) exist, so the answer is 1. Querying (14,8) finds no diagonal at distance 3, returning 0. Adding a second (11,2) and re-querying (11,10) gives 2, because corner (11,2) can now be chosen twice.

Constraints: coordinates in [0,1000] and at most 3000 calls total, so even scanning all stored points per count is fast.
k: The query is a corner; enumerate potential diagonal corners characterized by |Δx| = |Δy| > 0 — the remaining two corners are determined.
Ways multiply: cnt(diagonal) × cnt(corner A) × cnt(corner B), which is exactly how duplicates inflate counts.
Keep a list of unique points separate from their counts so duplicates are not rescanned.

a.n: Approach 1: Raw point list with linear corner searches
a.i: Store every added point in a plain list. To answer a count, consider each stored point as a possible diagonal corner; when it qualifies, rescan the list to tally occurrences of the two forced corners and multiply. Correct and simple, but each count may cost quadratic time in the number of stored points.
s: append every added point to a list.
On count(qx,qy): iterate stored points; skip those failing px != qx or |px−qx| != |py−qy|.
Count occurrences of (px, qy) and (qx, py) by scanning the list.
Accumulate product of the two tallies over all diagonals.
a.t: add O(1); count O(P^2) — each candidate diagonal rescans all P points for both corners

a.n: Approach 2: Frequency map over unique points (optimal)
a.i: Maintain a hash map from encoded coordinate to multiplicity plus a list of unique keys. Adding updates the map in O(1) (appending the key only when a point type first appears). Counting iterates unique points as diagonal candidates and multiplies the three multiplicities — no rescans, and duplicates are handled purely arithmetically. Coordinates fit in [0,1000], so key = x·1001 + y encodes pairs collision-free.
s: add(x,y): bump cnt[key] and append key to a unique list on first appearance.
count(qx,qy): for each unique point (px,py) require px != qx and |px−qx| == |py−qy|.
Add cnt[(px,py)] · cnt[(px,qy)] · cnt[(qx,py)] to the answer.
a.t: add O(1); count O(U) — one pass over U unique points with O(1) map lookups
a.sp: O(U) — frequency map plus unique-key list

## Wrap-up

Go straight to the frequency-map design after sketching the brute force — enumerating diagonal corners is the insight that keeps counting linear. Pitfalls: allowing px == qx, which would count degenerate zero-area squares; adding multiplicities instead of multiplying them; iterating the full multiset of points so duplicates waste work (or worse, miscounting); forgetting that a square admits two diagonals but only the one opposite the query matters here since the query is fixed as a corner. Edge cases: query coinciding with an added point (distance 0 must be rejected), all points collinear (answer 0), heavy duplication. Follow-ups: support rotated squares (enumerate pairs and verify distances), deletions, or unbounded coordinates (switch to hashing coordinate pairs directly).
